title: Treasure Island
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
ru: Юный Джим Хокинс, карта сокровищ, пираты и одноногий Джон Сильвер

chapters.title: Chapter 1. The Old Sea-Dog at the Admiral Benbow
chapters.text:
My name is Jim Hawkins. When I was a boy, my father and mother kept an inn called the Admiral Benbow, on the lonely coast of the west of England. Squire Trelawney, Dr Livesey and other gentlemen have asked me to write down the whole story of Treasure Island, from the beginning to the end. So I will start at the time when the old sea captain first came to live under our roof.

He was a tall, strong, brown man with a scar across one cheek. He came to our door with a heavy sea chest behind him, singing the old sea song that he sang so often afterwards:

“Fifteen men on the dead man’s chest,
Yo-ho-ho, and a bottle of rum!”

He called himself the captain, but his name was Billy Bones. He paid for a room with a few gold coins and said he would stay for a while. All day he walked along the cliffs with a telescope, and all evening he sat by the fire and drank rum. He hardly ever spoke, but when he did, everyone listened. He told terrible stories about hanging, storms at sea and wild deeds in the Spanish Main. Our visitors were frightened, but they kept coming back.

The captain paid me a silver fourpenny coin every month to watch for “a seafaring man with one leg”. He was clearly afraid of this man, and so was I. On stormy nights I dreamed about a monster with one leg who chased me over hedges and ditches.

My father was very ill that winter, and we did not dare to ask the captain for more money, although he stayed for months and never paid again.

One cold January morning a pale man with two fingers missing on his left hand came into the inn. He asked for his “mate Bill”. When the captain saw him, his face went grey.

“Black Dog!” he said.

The two men talked quietly for a while, then they began to shout. Then Black Dog ran out with blood on his shoulder. The captain fell to the floor. Dr Livesey, who was visiting my father, came and helped him.

“You have had a stroke,” said the doctor. “One more glass of rum, and you will die.”

Later that day, lying in bed, the captain told me the truth. “Jim, it is my sea chest they want,” he whispered. “I was the first mate of old Captain Flint, and I am the only one who knows the place. If they give me the black spot, go to the doctor.”

That same night my poor father died.

chapters.title: Chapter 2. The Black Spot and the Map
chapters.text:
The next afternoon I was standing at the door of the inn, thinking sad thoughts about my father, when I saw a strange figure coming slowly along the road. He was a blind man. He tapped the road in front of him with a stick,.

“Will any kind friend tell a poor blind man where he is?” he called.

“You are at the Admiral Benbow, my good man,” I said.

He held out his hand, and I took it. At once it closed on mine like iron. “Now, boy,” he said, “take me to the captain, or I will break your arm.”

I was so frightened that I obeyed. When the captain saw him, he looked sick with terror. The blind man put something into his hand and left the inn quickly. The captain opened his hand and looked at it.

“Ten o’clock!” he cried. “Six hours. We can do them yet!” He jumped to his feet, then he held his throat, and fell on his face on the floor. He was dead.

In his hand was a round piece of paper, black on one side. On the other side it said: “You have till ten tonight.”

My mother and I were terrified. The captain owed us money, so we decided to open his chest and take what he owed us, and then run to the village. Inside the chest there were old clothes, a pistol, some coins and a packet wrapped in oilcloth. My mother began to count out the money very slowly.

Suddenly we heard the tap-tap-tapping of the blind man’s stick on the frozen road, and then a whistle in the distance.

“I’ll take what I have,” said my mother, and I grabbed the oilcloth packet. We ran out into the fog and hid under a small bridge near the inn.

Soon seven or eight men ran up to the inn. The blind man, whose name was Pew, was shouting orders. They broke open the door and searched everything.

“It’s gone! Flint’s fist is gone!” somebody cried.

“It’s that boy!” screamed Pew. “Find him!”

At that moment we heard horses on the road. The pirates ran away, but blind Pew fell under the horses. He died immediately.

I took the packet to Dr Livesey, who was with Squire Trelawney. Together we opened it. Inside was a map of an island, with three red crosses on it and the words: “Bulk of treasure here.”

The squire was delighted. “Flint’s treasure!” he cried. “I will buy a ship in Bristol, and we will go and find it. Hawkins will be cabin boy, and you, Livesey, will be ship’s doctor!”

chapters.title: Chapter 3. Long John Silver
chapters.text:
A few weeks later the squire wrote to us from Bristol. He had bought a fine ship called the Hispaniola, and he had found a crew. The best news, he wrote, was that he had met an old sailor who kept a public house in Bristol. This man had only one leg, but he knew everyone in the port. He had agreed to be the ship’s cook, and he had helped the squire to find most of the sailors. His name was Long John Silver.

I said goodbye to my mother and travelled to Bristol. The squire sent me with a note to Silver’s inn, the Spy-glass. When I saw him, I was a little afraid. Had I found the one-legged man that Billy Bones had feared so much? But Silver was tall and strong, with a clean, pleasant face, and he walked on his crutch as easily as a bird. He was so friendly and cheerful that I decided he could not possibly be a pirate.

Silver had a parrot, which he called Captain Flint, after the famous pirate. It sat on his shoulder and screamed, “Pieces of eight! Pieces of eight!”

However, not everyone was happy. Captain Smollett, whom the squire had hired to command the ship, came to talk to us before we sailed.

“I don’t like this cruise,” he said. “I don’t like the men, and I don’t like the fact that every sailor on this ship seems to know more than I do. They know we are going for treasure. They even know about the map. Someone has been talking too much.”

The squire went red, because the someone was clearly himself. But the doctor listened carefully. Captain Smollett asked for the guns and gunpowder to be moved to the back of the ship, near our cabins, and he asked that only the gentlemen should keep the secret of the island.

Early the next morning we set sail. The voyage was mostly good. The ship sailed well, and the crew worked hard. Silver was very popular, and he was always kind to me.

On the last evening before we reached the island, I felt hungry and went to get an apple. There was a large barrel of apples on the deck, but only a few were left at the bottom, so I climbed right inside. While I was sitting there in the dark, a heavy man sat down against the barrel and began to talk. It was Silver. Before I had heard a dozen words, I was shaking with fear. I realised that the lives of all the honest men on board depended on me alone.

chapters.title: Chapter 4. What I Heard in the Apple Barrel
chapters.text:
“Flint was captain, and I was quartermaster, with my timber leg,” Silver was saying to a young sailor. “The same broadside that took off my leg took out old Pew’s eyes. I have saved my money, and I will live like a gentleman soon.”

In a few minutes I understood everything. Most of the crew were Flint’s old pirates. Silver had chosen them himself. They planned to let the captain sail the ship to the island and back, and to let the gentlemen find the treasure. Then they would kill them all and keep the gold.

“And when we have it,” asked another man called Israel Hands, “what shall we do with them?”

“Dead men don’t bite,” said Silver. “That is my view. But wait until I give the word.”

Then someone shouted from above, “Land ho!” Everyone ran to see, and I climbed quietly out of the barrel and joined them.

As soon as I could, I told Dr Livesey that I had terrible news. He took me to the captain’s cabin, where the squire and the captain were sitting, and I told them everything I had heard.

“Captain,” said the squire, “you were right, and I was wrong. I am an ass.”

We counted the honest men. There were the three gentlemen, three of the squire’s own servants, and myself. That was seven against nineteen. The captain decided that we must act as if we knew nothing and wait for a chance.

The next morning we anchored near the island. It was a grey, unfriendly place, with thick woods and high hills. For the first time they refused to obey orders, and the ship felt close to mutiny.

The captain had a clever idea. He told the crew that they could go ashore for the afternoon. The pirates were sure to go, because they thought the treasure was near. Silver agreed to lead them. Thirteen men went in the boats, and six stayed on the ship.

At that moment I did a foolish thing. I suddenly decided to go ashore too. I jumped into one of the boats just as it was leaving, and when we reached the beach I ran into the woods before anyone could stop me.

I was happy at first. But then I heard voices, and I hid in the bushes. I saw Silver talking to an honest sailor called Tom. Tom refused to join the pirates and turned to go. Silver threw his crutch at him and then killed him with his knife.

I ran as fast as I could, not caring where. And then I saw a strange figure jump behind a tree. It was not an animal. It was a man.

chapters.title: Chapter 5. The Man of the Island and the Stockade
chapters.text:
The man came out slowly and fell on his knees in front of me. His skin was burnt by the sun, his clothes were made of old sailcloth and goatskins, and his eyes were very bright.

“Who are you?” I asked.

“Ben Gunn,” he answered, in a rusty voice, like a door that has not been opened for years. “I’m poor Ben Gunn, I am. I haven’t spoken with a Christian these three years.”

He had sailed with Flint when the pirate buried his treasure with six men, who never came back. Later, Ben Gunn came back to the island on another ship and told the crew about the gold. They searched for twelve days and found nothing, so they left him on the island with a gun and a spade.

“You mustn’t think I’m poor, Jim,” he said with a secret smile. “I’m rich. And I’ll make you rich too, if you help me get home. Tell your squire that Ben Gunn wants only a thousand pounds and a ship home.”

Suddenly we heard the sound of a cannon from the sea, and then gunfire. I ran towards the sound. Above the trees I saw the British flag flying over an old wooden fort.

While I had been in the woods, my friends had left the ship in a small boat with guns and food. They had gone to the stockade, a strong wooden house surrounded by a high fence, which was marked on Flint’s map. The pirates had attacked them,.

When I climbed over the fence, they were very glad to see me. I told them about Ben Gunn, and the doctor was very interested.

The next morning Silver came to the stockade with a white flag. He sat down on the sand and offered a deal.

“Give us the map,” he said, “and we will take you home safely, or leave you on the island with food. Otherwise, you will all be dead.”

Captain Smollett laughed at him. “You can’t find the treasure, and you can’t sail the ship. Go back to your men, Silver. The next time I see you, I will put a bullet in your back.”

Silver was furious. “Before an hour’s out, I’ll stove in your old blockhouse like a rum barrel!” he shouted.

An hour later the pirates attacked from all sides. They climbed over the fence, and for a few minutes there was terrible fighting with swords and pistols. But we drove them back. When it was over, five pirates were dead, and we had lost two more men. The captain was badly wounded.

chapters.title: Chapter 6. My Sea Adventure
chapters.text:
After the battle, things were quiet for a while. In the afternoon the doctor took the map, put a pistol in his belt and walked out towards the woods. I guessed that he was going to find Ben Gunn.

I was hot, tired and bored in the stockade, and I began to plan another foolish adventure. Ben Gunn had told me that he had a small boat hidden near a white rock. I filled my pockets with bread and, when nobody was watching, I climbed over the fence and ran away.

I found the little boat. When it got dark, I paddled out towards the Hispaniola. My plan was to cut her anchor rope so that she would drift away and the pirates could not escape with her.

I reached the ship and cut the rope with my knife, one thread at a time. The ship began to drift. Then my little boat was caught by the current and pulled out to sea. Exhausted, I fell asleep.

When I woke up, it was daylight. To my surprise, the Hispaniola was close to me, sailing wildly in the wind with nobody at the wheel. I paddled to her and climbed on board.

On the deck I found the two pirates. One was dead. The other, Israel Hands, was badly hurt and weak from drinking.

“I am taking possession of this ship,” I told him. I pulled down the pirate flag and threw it into the sea. Hands agreed to help me steer the ship into a quiet bay.

But while I was busy, I noticed that he had taken a long knife and hidden it in his coat. I watched him carefully. When the ship reached the shallow water, he suddenly attacked me. I ran and climbed up the mast, loading my pistols as I climbed. Hands followed me slowly, with the knife between his teeth.

“One more step, Mr Hands,” I said, “and I will blow your brains out! Dead men don’t bite, you know.”

He stopped. Then, with a quick movement, he threw the knife. It hit my shoulder and pinned me to the mast. At the same moment both my pistols fired, almost by themselves. Israel Hands fell with a cry into the water and did not come up again.

I pulled myself free, bleeding but not seriously hurt. The ship was safe in the bay. As night fell, I walked back through the woods to the stockade and climbed over the fence in the dark.

Suddenly a sharp voice screamed, “Pieces of eight! Pieces of eight!” It was Silver’s parrot. The stockade was full of pirates.

chapters.title: Chapter 7. Prisoner of the Pirates
chapters.text:
Somebody lit a torch, and I saw six pirates around me. Long John Silver sat on a barrel, smoking his pipe.

“So here’s Jim Hawkins,” he said pleasantly. “Dropped in, like, eh? Well, come, I take that friendly.”

He told me that my friends had left the stockade. The doctor had come to them with a white flag and had given them the stockade, the food and, most surprising of all, the treasure map. My friends had walked away, and nobody knew where they were.

I felt sick, but I decided to be brave. “Well,” I said, “I have nothing to lose now. I’ll tell you something. It was I who heard you in the apple barrel, and I told my friends. It was I who cut the ship’s rope and killed the men on board. And I have taken her where you will never see her again. Kill me if you like, or let me live, and I will help you when you are on trial for piracy.”

The pirates were furious and wanted to kill me at once. But Silver stood up for me. “I like that boy,” he said. “He is more a man than any pair of rats of you.”

The men went outside to talk. When they came back, one of them gave Silver the black spot. They no longer wanted him as their leader. But Silver was too clever for them. He threw the map on the floor in front of them.

The men jumped on it like cats on a mouse. Silver was captain again.

Later, when we were alone, Silver spoke to me quietly. “Jim, I’ve lost the ship, and I know it. I’ll save your life from the men if I can. But you must save Long John from hanging.”

I understood then that Silver was playing a double game. He wanted to be on the winning side, whichever side it was.

The next morning the doctor came to the stockade to look after the sick and wounded pirates. He was angry to see me there.

“Jim,” said the doctor, “it was very wrong of you to run away when the captain was hurt. But you have saved our lives again and again. Now we will save yours. Run! Jump over the fence, and we will run together.”

“No,” I said. “I gave Silver my word. I cannot break it.”

The doctor looked at me sadly. Then I told him where the ship was, and his face changed.

“Every step, it’s you that saves our lives,” he said. Then he turned to Silver. “Keep the boy close to you, Silver. And when you find the treasure, look out for trouble.”

chapters.title: Chapter 8. The Treasure
chapters.text:
After breakfast the pirates set off to find the treasure. Silver had a rope tied around my waist, and he pulled me along like a dancing bear. The pirates followed the directions on the back of the map: “Tall tree, Spy-glass shoulder, bearing a point to the north.”

On the way, we found a human skeleton lying on the ground. Its long bony arms pointed straight in the direction of the treasure. It was one of Flint’s six men. Flint had used the body as a sign.

The pirates were frightened. They began to talk in low voices about Flint’s ghost. Suddenly, from the trees, a thin, high voice began to sing:

“Fifteen men on the dead man’s chest,
Yo-ho-ho, and a bottle of rum!”

The men went white with fear. “It’s Flint!” one of them cried. But Silver was not afraid. “That’s not Flint,” he said. “I know that voice. It’s Ben Gunn!” The men laughed at their fear and went on.

At last they found the tall tree and ran towards it, shouting with excitement. And then they stopped. In front of them was a large hole in the ground. It was old, and grass was growing at the bottom. There was a broken spade and some pieces of wooden boxes. The treasure was gone.

The pirates turned on Silver. They were ready to kill us both. Silver gave me a pistol. At that moment three shots came from the trees. Two pirates fell, and the others ran away. The doctor, one of our men, and Ben Gunn came running out of the woods.

Ben Gunn had found the treasure long ago, and he had carried it, bit by bit, to his cave on the other side of the island. That was why the doctor had given the useless map to Silver.

We spent several days carrying the gold to the ship. We left the three last pirates on the island with food, guns and tools. Silver came with us. The doctor had promised not to hand him over to the law.

On the way home we stopped at a port in South America. One night Silver escaped with a bag of money.

We all received a good share of the treasure. Ben Gunn got a thousand pounds and spent it all in nineteen days. Nothing more was ever heard of Silver.

The rest of the treasure is still on the island, but oxen and ropes would not bring me back there. The worst dreams I ever have are when I hear the sea breaking on its coast, or when I wake up with Captain Flint’s sharp voice in my ears: “Pieces of eight! Pieces of eight!”
